abstract: | 
  Schools are key spaces of meritocratic socialization, yet little is known about how students conceive meritocracy and how these conceptions relate to the acceptance of privilege. Although several studies have suggested that beliefs in meritocracy are opposed to support for privilege, the evidence is mostly based on adult samples and unidimensional measures. In the present paper we surveyed Chilean students in 6th and 9th grade (Wave 1: N = 846) and again in 7th and 10th grade (Wave 2: N = 662), addressing not only the dimensionality of meritocratic and privilege beliefs, but also their longitudinal and cross-sectional measurement equivalence. We found that meritocracy and privilege are distinct dimensions, with weak and inconsistent associations across groups. Furthermore, secondary students were more skeptical than primary students about meritocracy. The study highlights the role of developmental and contextual factors in shaping students' beliefs about social inequalities.
  \medskip
  
  **Keywords**: Meritocracy · Privilege · Schools · Measurement invariance · Socialization · Chile
